column2: Samuel dies, all Israel gathers and mourns, and burial is at his house in Armathaim; David then descends to Maan's wilderness. Maan is not replaced with Paran.

The very great man resides in Maan with flocks at Carmel, three thousand sheep and one thousand goats, and shearing there; his wealth is expressed by the narrative quantities rather than a modern value.
Nabal and Abigail are named, her understanding and beauty contrast with his harshness and evil practices, and doglike remains the selected final characterization.
column3: Doglike follows kynikos, not an unmarked Calebite genealogy or a philosophical school identification.

column2: David in the wilderness hears of the Carmelite's shearing; the renewed identification connects the request to the stated occasion.
Ten young men are sent to Carmel with commands to approach Nabal and inquire about peace in David's name. The named sender governs the greeting.
To the seasons is retained before wishes of wellbeing for Nabal, his house and all possessions.
column3: The eis horas greeting is lexically and idiomatically unresolved; it is not silently converted to long life or a modern seasonal greeting.

column2: Now behold introduces the shearing report, followed by shepherds' companionship, non-hindrance and absence of imposed orders during the full Carmel period.

Nabal is told to ask his servants; favorable reception on a good day supports the request for whatever his hand finds for his son David. Son is a relational appeal in the speech, not a genealogical claim.
The messengers transmit all the words in David's name, then a singular he springs up, leading into Nabal's reply.
column3: Nabal is the likely implicit rising subject from the continuation; the selected singular is not changed to the messengers stopping or waiting.

column2: Nabal's two identity questions compare David with today's many slaves departing each master; the dismissive analogy remains the speaker's claim.
Nabal lists his loaves, wine and slaughtered offerings, with sheep and shearers, and rejects giving to men of unknown origin.
column3: The sheep phrase's attachment is compressed; the inherited apposition to the slaughtered offerings is provisional rather than a resolved reconstruction of the sentence.

column2: Turning onto their way, returning, coming and reporting all remain; the repeated travel verbs are not collapsed solely for variety.
David orders each man to gird a sword; about four hundred follow him and two hundred stay with equipment. No added girding narrative is imported.
A servant reports with Behold that David sent a blessing mission and Nabal turned away; turning is retained without replacing it with a differently worded insult verb.
The men are very good, neither hinder nor impose orders, throughout companionship; the field clause continues into the wall comparison of verse 16.
The men are like a wall by night and day during all the shared shepherding days. The protection image and repeated duration remain.
Abigail must know and see what to do because evil is determined against master and house; the pestilent-son description explains inability to speak to him.

Abigail hastens with two hundred loaves, two wine vessels, five prepared sheep, five oiphi of barley meal, one gomor of raisins and two hundred fig cakes on donkeys. All six quantities remain unconverted.
The servants go ahead while Behold introduces her following; she does not tell her husband. Both ordered movement and withheld information remain.
Her covered descent on the donkey meets David's descending company; there were carries the presentative encounter, followed by the explicit meeting.
David says perhaps he guarded for an unjust man, denied ordering any taking and received evil for good. Perhaps and the injustice reading are not replaced with surely in vain.
David invokes a self-directed divine curse if any of Nabal's wall-urinating persons remains by morning. The bodily idiom and scope of the violent vow remain without euphemism or added detail.
Abigail sees, hurries, jumps down, falls face-first before David and bows on the ground; the feet phrase continues in verse 24.
At David's feet she takes the wrong upon herself and asks permission to speak into his ears and be heard, repeating handmaid. Ordinary human address is maintained.
She asks David not to set his heart on the pestilent man, explains Nabal's name through folly and denies seeing the messengers herself. The explanation remains within her speech.
The Lord's life and David's soul are invoked, divine restraint from innocent blood and saving one's hand is stated, and a wish makes enemies like Nabal.
column3: The kathos clause's connection with the oath is compressed in the inherited English; saving your hand for yourself remains a difficult idiom rather than an added explicit revenge paraphrase.

column2: The gift is called this blessing and is to be received and distributed to David's attendant young men; the lord/handmaid social register remains.
Propose For before the emphatic promise of a faithful house, keeping its explanatory link to the forgiveness request. The Lord's war and never finding evil in David remain.
column3: Surely expresses the cognate making construction; the speech is not recast as a narrator's unconditional assessment of David's entire life.

column2: A rising pursuer seeks David's soul, which is bound in the bond of life beside the Lord God; David, addressed in second person, will sling the enemies' soul in the sling's midst.
column3: The selected slinging subject is you, not God; singular soul with plural enemies and the bond/sling imagery remain without theological expansion.

column2: The Lord's fulfillment of all spoken good and appointment of David as leader introduce the continued sentence about absence of a stumbling block.
Innocent blood without cause and saving one's own hand are named as the avoided abomination/stumbling block; future divine goodness and remembering the handmaid to benefit her remain.
column3: The repeated hand-saving idiom and its relation to self-vengeance remain provisional; the text does not replace the image with a new abstract verdict.

column2: David blesses the Lord God of Israel for sending Abigail today, on this day, to meet him. The doubled day is retained rather than removed for economy.
Her manner and she herself are blessed for preventing bloodguilt and self-hand-saving today, on this day; the corresponding claims echo her appeal.
column3: Manner for tropos and bloodguilt for plural bloods are contextual choices, not complete lexical definitions.

column2: The Lord's life, restraint from harming Abigail, a counterfactual without her haste and the recalled no-survivor oath remain.
column3: The selected then I said sequence is awkward within the conditional; inherited quotation boundaries are editorial and leave the syntax unresolved rather than silently normalizing it.

column2: David receives all from her hand, sends her home in peace and declares hearing her voice and favoring her face. Both personal acceptance images remain.
The presentative royal-like drinking feast, merry heart, extreme drunkenness and Abigail's silence about small or great matters until morning remain.
After sobriety she reports, his heart dies within him and he becomes like stone. The physical imagery is retained without a medical diagnosis.
About ten days later the Lord strikes Nabal and he dies; both approximate interval and explicit divine agency remain.
David blesses the Lord for judging reproach, preserving His servant from evil's hand and returning Nabal's evil onto his head; the marriage initiative follows as a separate action.
David's servants arrive at Carmel and state their commission to take Abigail as his wife; the reported offer does not omit sender or destination relationship.
Abigail rises, bows face to earth and presents herself as handmaid to wash the servants' feet. The deferential reply and servant-of-servants relation remain.
She mounts the donkey with five girls following, goes after David's servants and becomes his wife; the companions' number remains explicit.
David also takes Ahinoam from Jezreel and both women are his wives. The text's plural marital situation is retained without harmonizing away either woman.
Saul gives his daughter Michal, still described as David's wife, to Palti son of Laish from Romma. The selected locality and both relational descriptions remain.
